senses: Being the best or most typical example of its kind; above all others.

etymology: From French par excellence, literally "by excellence," meaning "preeminently." It has been used in English since the late 1600s.

conversation.text: She's the storyteller par excellence in our family. Every holiday, we wait for her stories.
New Orleans is the party town par excellence.

core.definition: Being the best or most typical example of its kind; above all others.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the last syllable: ek-suh-LAHNS, with "ah" as in "father." "Par" sounds like the golf word.

nuance.connotation: Positive; high praise that presents someone or something as the model of its type.
nuance.usage_note: Comes right after the noun it describes: "a host par excellence," "the American sport par excellence." It is fairly common in writing, reviews, and speeches, less common in casual talk. Usually not italicized in American writing. It means "the best example of," not just "excellent," so it sounds odd after a noun that is not a type ("a meal par excellence" is fine; "he did it par excellence" is not).

distinctions.note: "Quintessential" goes before the noun ("the quintessential New Yorker"); "par excellence" goes after it ("a New Yorker par excellence"). The meaning is close.
"Excellent" just means very good; "par excellence" says something is the supreme example of its kind.

examples.everyday: My grandmother was a baker par excellence; nobody made better pie.
examples.professional: Our new CFO is a negotiator par excellence, and the deal shows it.
examples.analytical: The novel is the bourgeois art form par excellence, according to several critics.

nuance.analogy: Like the photo next to the word in a picture dictionary: the one example everyone else is measured against.
nuance.etymology: From French par excellence, literally "by excellence," meaning "preeminently." It has been used in English since the late 1600s.
common_mistakes: Putting it before the noun ("a par excellence chef"); it follows the noun: "a chef par excellence."
Pronouncing "excellence" the English way with stress on the first syllable (EK-suh-lens); Americans usually say ek-suh-LAHNS.
Using it as an adverb meaning "excellently" ("she sang par excellence").

senses: The most important reason for someone or something to exist; the main purpose of a person, group, or thing.

etymology: From French raison d'être, literally "reason for being." It came into English in the mid-1800s.

conversation.text: Honestly, coffee is my raison d'être before 9 a.m.
Helping small businesses is the whole raison d'être of this program.

core.definition: The most important reason for someone or something to exist; the main purpose of a person, group, or thing.

pronunciation.tip: Two parts: RAY-zohn, then DET-ruh. Stress "det." The final "-tre" is a light "truh" or just "tr."

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; often a little grand, and sometimes used jokingly about small things.
nuance.usage_note: Used in essays, journalism, and serious talk about purpose: "the company's raison d'être," "his raison d'être." People also use it playfully for a passion ("golf is his raison d'être"). Usually not italicized in American writing, and the circumflex is often dropped (raison d'etre). The plural, rarely needed, is raisons d'être.

distinctions.note: A reason explains why something happened; a raison d'être is the deep purpose that justifies something existing at all.
"Mission" is the everyday business word; "raison d'être" sounds more literary and personal.

examples.everyday: After the kids left home, she felt she had lost her raison d'être.
examples.professional: Customer service is the raison d'être of our support team, so response time comes first.
examples.analytical: Once the Cold War ended, critics argued that the alliance had lost its raison d'être.

nuance.analogy: Like the engine in a car: take it out and the thing has no reason to be there.
nuance.etymology: From French raison d'être, literally "reason for being." It came into English in the mid-1800s.
common_mistakes: Spelling it "raison d'etre" with no apostrophe or as one word; the apostrophe stays: d'être.
Pronouncing "raison" like the dried fruit "raisin"; it is RAY-zohn.
Using it to mean a simple cause ("the raison d'être of the accident").

senses: Required by fashion, custom, or etiquette; expected as the proper thing in a certain setting.

etymology: From French de rigueur, literally "of strictness," meaning "required." It came into English in the early 1800s.

conversation.text: Black tie is de rigueur at the gala, so I need to rent a tux.
Apparently, oat milk is de rigueur at this coffee shop.

core.definition: Required by fashion, custom, or etiquette; expected as the proper thing in a certain setting.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the last syllable: rih-GUR. "De" is a soft "duh." Do not pronounce it like the English word "rigor."

nuance.connotation: Neutral; often slightly ironic about rules of style that people follow without question.
nuance.usage_note: Most often used about clothing, manners, and trends: "Suits are de rigueur on the trading floor." It usually follows a linking verb ("is de rigueur"), and is sometimes used before a noun in a hyphenated form, though that is rare. It is common in fashion and lifestyle writing and often has a light, wry tone. Usually not italicized.

distinctions.note: "Mandatory" is required by rule or law; "de rigueur" is required by custom or fashion.
"In vogue" means popular right now; "de rigueur" means so expected that not doing it stands out.

examples.everyday: Sunglasses are de rigueur at the beach in July.
examples.professional: A short thank-you email after an interview is de rigueur in most industries.
examples.analytical: By the 1960s, a television set was de rigueur in middle-class American homes.

nuance.analogy: Like wearing a jersey to a team's home game: no one makes you, but you would stand out without it.
nuance.etymology: From French de rigueur, literally "of strictness," meaning "required." It came into English in the early 1800s.
common_mistakes: Spelling it "de rigeur"; the French has "gueu": rigueur.
Pronouncing it "duh RIG-er" like "rigor."
Using it to mean "strict" or "rigorous" ("a de rigueur teacher").

senses: A person or thing that someone especially dislikes, fears, or keeps having trouble with.

etymology: From French bête noire, literally "black beast." It came into English in the mid-1800s.

conversation.text: Parallel parking is my bête noire. I'll walk three blocks to avoid it.
That senator has been the bête noire of the tech industry for years.

core.definition: A person or thing that someone especially dislikes, fears, or keeps having trouble with.

pronunciation.tip: Two beats: bet NWAHR. "Noire" starts with a quick "nw" sound, like "n" plus the "w" in "water."

nuance.connotation: Negative toward the thing named, but the phrase itself is often used with humor.
nuance.usage_note: Common in journalism and educated speech: "Grammar mistakes are her bête noire." It can name a person (a long-time opponent) or a thing (a pet hate or a persistent weakness). Usually not italicized; accents are often dropped in casual writing (bete noire). Plural: bêtes noires.

distinctions.note: A pet peeve is a small annoyance; a bête noire is stronger, something you really dread or hate.
"Nemesis" is an enemy or rival who defeats you; "bête noire" can also be a thing, like math or taxes.

examples.everyday: Spiders have always been my bête noire.
examples.professional: Spreadsheets are my bête noire, so I hand the budget to Nina.
examples.analytical: Inflation became the bête noire of the administration in its second year.

nuance.analogy: Like the one monster in a video game you always lose to: you know it is coming and you dread it.
nuance.etymology: From French bête noire, literally "black beast." It came into English in the mid-1800s.
common_mistakes: Writing "bete noir" without the final e; noire is feminine to match bête.
Pronouncing "noire" as "noy-er" or "nor"; say NWAHR.

senses: Something that has already been done or decided before the people affected could object, so they have no choice but to accept it.

etymology: From French fait accompli, literally "accomplished fact." It came into English in the mid-1800s.

conversation.text: They didn't ask us. By the time we heard about the merger, it was a fait accompli.
I'd rather discuss it now than present you with a fait accompli later.

core.definition: Something that has already been done or decided before the people affected could object, so they have no choice but to accept it.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the very end: uh-kahm-PLEE. "Fait" can be "fayt" or "fet"; both are heard.

nuance.connotation: Usually negative: it suggests people were left out of a decision on purpose.
nuance.usage_note: Common in news, politics, and office talk, often with "present someone with a fait accompli" or "treat something as a fait accompli." It carries a sense of unfairness or power: the decision was made without consultation. Usually not italicized. Plural: faits accomplis.

distinctions.note: "Done deal" is the casual American equivalent; "fait accompli" is more formal and stresses that others had no say.
A foregone conclusion is certain to happen; a fait accompli has already happened.

collocations: present someone with a fait accompli
treat it as a fait accompli

examples.everyday: Mom had already booked the trip, so our vacation was a fait accompli.
examples.professional: The board presented the staff with a fait accompli: the office would close in March.
examples.analytical: Rapid construction of the settlements created a fait accompli that negotiators could not easily undo.

nuance.analogy: Like finding the cake already baked and served when you were asked what flavor you wanted.
nuance.etymology: From French fait accompli, literally "accomplished fact." It came into English in the mid-1800s.
common_mistakes: Spelling it "fait accompi" or "fete accompli"; the words are fait and accompli.
Using it for something merely likely ("the win is a fait accompli" before the game); strictly, it is already done.

senses: The strange feeling that you have already experienced exactly what is happening now; also, a sense that something is tiresomely familiar.

etymology: From French déjà vu, literally "already seen." French researchers used it for the sensation in the late 1800s, and it entered English in the early 1900s.

conversation.text: Whoa, I just had the weirdest déjà vu. I feel like we've had this exact conversation before.
Another rate hike? This is total déjà vu.

core.definition: The strange feeling that you have already experienced exactly what is happening now; also, a sense that something is tiresomely familiar.

pronunciation.tip: Say day-zhah VOO. The middle "j" is the soft "zh" sound in "measure," not the "j" in "jam."

nuance.connotation: Neutral; in the second sense, mildly weary or ironic.
nuance.usage_note: Very common in everyday American speech: "I'm getting déjà vu," "a sense of déjà vu." The second sense ("we've seen this before") is common in news and sports. Not italicized. Accents are often dropped (deja vu), especially in headlines and texting. Yogi Berra's joke "It's déjà vu all over again" is widely quoted.

distinctions.note: A flashback is a memory of something that really happened; déjà vu is a feeling that the present has happened before.
Nostalgia is fondness for the past; déjà vu is a sense of repetition, often unsettling.

examples.everyday: Walking into the old school gave me déjà vu.
examples.professional: The second budget crisis gave the team a strong sense of déjà vu.
examples.analytical: Researchers think déjà vu may arise from a brief mismatch between familiarity and recall in memory.

nuance.analogy: Like hearing a song on the radio and being sure you already know the next line, even though you have never heard it.
nuance.etymology: From French déjà vu, literally "already seen." French researchers used it for the sensation in the late 1800s, and it entered English in the early 1900s.
common_mistakes: Spelling it "deja vous" or "day ja vu"; the second word is vu.
Saying "I had a déjà vu" with "a"; Americans usually say "I had déjà vu" or "a sense of déjà vu."
Pronouncing the j as in "jam"; it is "zh."

senses: A final blow or event that ends something that was already failing; originally, a death blow given to end suffering.

etymology: From French coup de grâce, literally "stroke of mercy," the blow that killed a wounded person to end their pain. It came into English in the late 1600s.

conversation.text: That last three-pointer was the coup de grâce. The game was over after that.
The store was struggling, and the new mall was the coup de grâce.

core.definition: A final blow or event that ends something that was already failing; originally, a death blow given to end suffering.

pronunciation.tip: Say koo duh GRAHS. Pronounce the final s. "Coup" has no p sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative for whatever is ending; the phrase sounds dramatic and decisive.
nuance.usage_note: Used in news, sports, and business: "deliver the coup de grâce," "the coup de grâce came when..." The thing it ends is usually already weak. Usually not italicized; often written without the accent (coup de grace).

distinctions.note: "The last straw" is a small thing that finally makes someone lose patience; "coup de grâce" is a decisive blow that ends something.
Close in meaning; "knockout blow" is plain English, "coup de grâce" adds the idea of finishing something already doomed.

examples.everyday: My phone was already cracked, and dropping it in the pool was the coup de grâce.
examples.professional: Losing its biggest client delivered the coup de grâce to the struggling agency.
examples.analytical: Historians often treat the 1929 crash as the coup de grâce for an already fragile banking system.

nuance.analogy: Like the last gust of wind that topples a tree whose roots had already rotted.
nuance.etymology: From French coup de grâce, literally "stroke of mercy," the blow that killed a wounded person to end their pain. It came into English in the late 1600s.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it "koo de GRAH," as if it were "gras" (fat); the s is pronounced: GRAHS.
Spelling it "coup de gras."
Saying "the final coup de grâce" is redundant to some editors, since the phrase already means a final blow.

senses: The best, most impressive part of something, such as the main dish of a meal or the highlight of a collection or show.

etymology: From French pièce de résistance, literally "piece of resistance," meaning the solid, filling main dish of a meal. It came into English in the late 1700s.

conversation.text: The appetizers were nice, but the brisket was the pièce de résistance.
And now, the pièce de résistance: the cake I spent all day on!

core.definition: The best, most impressive part of something, such as the main dish of a meal or the highlight of a collection or show.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the end: ruh-zee-STAHNS. "Pièce" is pee-ES, two quick syllables.

nuance.connotation: Positive; often said with a playful, showy flourish.
nuance.usage_note: Used for the highlight of a meal, event, collection, or project, often announced with drama: "And the pièce de résistance..." It is common in food writing and also used jokingly in conversation. Usually not italicized; accents often dropped (piece de resistance). Plural: pièces de résistance.

distinctions.note: A centerpiece is the central feature; the pièce de résistance is specifically the most impressive one, often saved for last.
"Highlight" is plain and neutral; "pièce de résistance" adds a sense of grand presentation.

collocations: and now, the pièce de résistance

examples.everyday: The pièce de résistance of the garden is a hundred-year-old oak.
examples.professional: The live demo was the pièce de résistance of our pitch.
examples.analytical: The museum's pièce de résistance is a rare first edition of the Declaration's printed text.

nuance.analogy: Like the fireworks finale: everything before it is good, but this is the part people remember.
nuance.etymology: From French pièce de résistance, literally "piece of resistance," meaning the solid, filling main dish of a meal. It came into English in the late 1700s.
common_mistakes: Using it to mean "resistance" or opposition; it has nothing to do with resisting.
Pronouncing "résistance" like English "resistance" (rih-ZIS-tuns); Americans usually say ruh-zee-STAHNS.

senses: An issue, case, or person that attracts wide public attention and strong debate, often becoming a symbol for a larger cause.

etymology: From French cause célèbre, literally "famous case," first used for famous trials. It came into English in the 1700s.

conversation.text: Her firing became a cause célèbre online. Everyone had an opinion.
The case turned into a cause célèbre for free-speech groups.

core.definition: An issue, case, or person that attracts wide public attention and strong debate, often becoming a symbol for a larger cause.

pronunciation.tip: Say kawz say-LEB, stressing "leb." Some people add a light "-ruh" at the end (say-LEB-ruh); both are heard.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; suggests intense, sometimes passionate public attention.
nuance.usage_note: Used mostly in journalism and educated writing: "become a cause célèbre," "a cause célèbre among activists." It usually refers to a specific case or person that stands for a wider issue. Usually not italicized. Plural: causes célèbres.

distinctions.note: A cause is a goal people support (like clean water); a cause célèbre is a particular case that draws huge public attention.
A scandal involves wrongdoing; a cause célèbre may involve no wrongdoing at all, just intense public interest.

examples.everyday: The neighborhood's fight to save the old theater became a local cause célèbre.
examples.professional: The whistleblower's lawsuit turned into a cause célèbre in the industry.
examples.analytical: The Dreyfus affair is the classic cause célèbre of modern European history.

nuance.analogy: Like a single pebble in a pond that sends ripples across the whole surface.
nuance.etymology: From French cause célèbre, literally "famous case," first used for famous trials. It came into English in the 1700s.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it "cause celebrity" or "cause SEL-uh-bray."
Using it to mean any good cause ("recycling is my cause célèbre"); it is a specific, famous case.

senses: A person, often young and talented, whose bold or shocking behavior or ideas upset the people around them, especially in art, politics, or a profession.

etymology: From French enfant terrible, literally "terrible child." It came into English in the mid-1800s.

conversation.text: He was the enfant terrible of the fashion world in the nineties.
Our new intern is a bit of an enfant terrible. She questioned the CEO in her first meeting.

core.definition: A person, often young and talented, whose bold or shocking behavior or ideas upset the people around them, especially in art, politics, or a profession.

pronunciation.tip: Stress "REE": ahn-fahn teh-REE-bluh. "Terrible" is said the French way, not like English "terrible."

nuance.connotation: Mixed; it admits the person is talented while noting they are provocative or difficult.
nuance.usage_note: Common in arts, media, and tech journalism: "the enfant terrible of American cinema." It describes an adult, not a misbehaving child. Usually not italicized. Plural: enfants terribles.

distinctions.note: A rebel fights authority; an enfant terrible is usually a gifted insider who shocks their own field.
"Bad boy" is the casual American term; "enfant terrible" sounds more cultured and is used for any gender.

examples.everyday: My cousin was the family's enfant terrible, always saying what no one else would.
examples.professional: The startup's founder plays the enfant terrible, but investors still trust his numbers.
examples.analytical: Critics once dismissed the composer as an enfant terrible; now his work is part of the standard repertoire.

nuance.analogy: Like a brilliant chef who serves dessert first just to see the reaction.
nuance.etymology: From French enfant terrible, literally "terrible child." It came into English in the mid-1800s.
common_mistakes: Using it for an actual badly behaved child; in English it describes an adult provocateur.
Pronouncing "terrible" the English way (TER-uh-bul).

senses: The idea that people with wealth, power, or privilege have a duty to act generously and responsibly toward others.

etymology: From French noblesse oblige, literally "nobility obligates." It came into English in the 1830s.

conversation.text: His family funds the town library out of a sense of noblesse oblige.
I don't want charity dressed up as noblesse oblige. I want a fair wage.

core.definition: The idea that people with wealth, power, or privilege have a duty to act generously and responsibly toward others.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the end: uh-BLEEZH, ending in the "zh" sound of "measure."

nuance.connotation: Mixed; positive when it means duty and generosity, critical when it suggests condescension from the privileged.
nuance.usage_note: Used in essays, politics, and discussions of philanthropy: "a sense of noblesse oblige." Today it is often used with some skepticism, implying the generosity comes from above. Usually not italicized.

distinctions.note: Philanthropy is the act of giving; noblesse oblige is the sense of duty that motivates the privileged to give.
Paternalism means controlling people for their own good; noblesse oblige is about obligation, though critics see the two as related.

examples.everyday: As the oldest, she felt a kind of noblesse oblige to help her siblings with tuition.
examples.professional: The firm's pro bono work comes partly from noblesse oblige and partly from good public relations.
examples.analytical: Some historians describe early American philanthropy as noblesse oblige adapted to industrial wealth.

nuance.analogy: Like the strongest kid on the team carrying the heavy gear because they can.
nuance.etymology: From French noblesse oblige, literally "nobility obligates." It came into English in the 1830s.
common_mistakes: Spelling it "noblesse obliged" or "noblese oblige."
Using it to mean the privileges of the rich rather than their duties.

senses: On the contrary; used to disagree, often playfully, with what someone just said.

etymology: From French au contraire, literally "to the contrary." It has been used in English for centuries; today it is mostly a playful reply.

conversation.text: "You're never on time." "Au contraire! I was early on Tuesday."
Boring? Au contraire, the second half was the best part.

core.definition: On the contrary; used to disagree, often playfully, with what someone just said.

pronunciation.tip: Say oh kahn-TRAIR, stressing "trair." "Au" sounds like "oh."

nuance.connotation: Light and playful; often a mock-fancy way to contradict someone.
nuance.usage_note: In American conversation, it is mainly a humorous or theatrical reply that starts a contradiction: "Au contraire, my friend." It is rare in formal writing, where "on the contrary" is used. Some speakers say "au contraire, mon frère" as a rhyming joke. Not italicized in casual writing.

distinctions.note: "On the contrary" is the standard English phrase for serious writing; "au contraire" is mostly playful.
"Actually" is the plain everyday way to correct someone; "au contraire" adds a mock-formal flourish.

examples.everyday: "You hate cooking." "Au contraire, I just hate dishes."
examples.professional: Au contraire, the data shows sales went up after the price change.
examples.analytical: The author's reply was essentially au contraire: the evidence, she argued, pointed the other way.

nuance.analogy: Like turning a coin over with a grin to show the other side.
nuance.etymology: From French au contraire, literally "to the contrary." It has been used in English for centuries; today it is mostly a playful reply.
common_mistakes: Spelling it "oh contraire" or "au contrare."
Using it in serious formal writing, where it can sound flippant; use "on the contrary."

senses: A person who enjoys life's pleasures, especially good food, drink, and company.

etymology: From French bon vivant, literally "one who lives well." It came into English in the late 1600s.

conversation.text: Uncle Ray is a real bon vivant. He knows every good restaurant in town.
Look at you, ordering champagne on a Tuesday. Such a bon vivant.

core.definition: A person who enjoys life's pleasures, especially good food, drink, and company.

pronunciation.tip: Say bahn vee-VAHNT. Americans usually pronounce the final t, though the French does not.

nuance.connotation: Mostly positive and affectionate; sometimes hints at indulgence.
nuance.usage_note: Used in profiles, obituaries, and friendly description: "a bon vivant and generous host." It is warmer than "glutton" and more social than "foodie." Usually not italicized. Plural: bons vivants (or bon vivants in casual use).

distinctions.note: A foodie is passionate about food; a bon vivant enjoys good living in general, including drink and company.
An epicure has refined, discriminating taste; a bon vivant is more about enjoyment and sociability.
"Bon viveur" means the same and is mainly British; Americans say "bon vivant."

examples.everyday: My grandfather was a bon vivant who never missed a dinner party.
examples.professional: The restaurant critic, a lifelong bon vivant, wrote about meals the way others write about travel.
examples.analytical: The memoir paints its author as a bon vivant whose generosity hid serious money troubles.

nuance.analogy: Like someone who treats every dinner as a small celebration.
nuance.etymology: From French bon vivant, literally "one who lives well." It came into English in the late 1600s.
common_mistakes: Spelling it "bon vivand" or "bonvivant" as one word.
Using it as an adjective ("a bon vivant lifestyle") is accepted by many, but it is chiefly a noun for a person.

senses: Have a good trip; said to someone who is leaving on a journey.

etymology: From French bon voyage, literally "good journey." It has been used in English for centuries and became common in the 1800s.

conversation.text: Bon voyage! Send me pictures from Rome.
We're having a little bon voyage party for Mia before she moves to Tokyo.

core.definition: Have a good trip; said to someone who is leaving on a journey.

pronunciation.tip: Americans usually say bahn voy-AHZH; a more French version is bohn vwah-YAHZH. End with the "zh" sound of "measure."

nuance.connotation: Warm and friendly; slightly festive.
nuance.usage_note: A very common, cheerful farewell for trips, especially long or exciting ones. It is also used as an adjective before a noun: "a bon voyage card," "a bon voyage party." Not italicized. It is not used for short daily departures like going to work.

distinctions.note: "Have a safe trip" is the plain American way; "bon voyage" is more festive and often used for big journeys.
"Farewell" is a general, somewhat formal goodbye; "bon voyage" specifically wishes someone a good trip.

examples.everyday: We waved from the dock and shouted, "Bon voyage!"
examples.professional: The office signed a bon voyage card for Luis before his transfer to London.
examples.analytical: The phrase bon voyage often appears in travel advertising to suggest glamour and adventure.

nuance.analogy: Like tossing confetti at someone as they step onto the ship.
nuance.etymology: From French bon voyage, literally "good journey." It has been used in English for centuries and became common in the 1800s.
common_mistakes: Spelling it "bon voyagé" or "bonvoyage."
Using it for someone who is just going home for the night; it suits trips.

senses: That's life; used to accept a disappointment or something that cannot be changed.

etymology: From French c'est la vie, literally "that is life." It has been common in English since about the early 1900s.

conversation.text: The flight got canceled. Oh well, c'est la vie.
You didn't get the part this time, but c'est la vie. There will be other auditions.

core.definition: That's life; used to accept a disappointment or something that cannot be changed.

pronunciation.tip: Three quick words: say luh VEE. "C'est" sounds like "say." Many people say "lah" for the middle word.

nuance.connotation: Resigned but calm; usually takes a shrug-it-off attitude.
nuance.usage_note: Common in casual speech and texting after a small setback. It suggests calm acceptance, sometimes with humor. It can sound dismissive if used about someone else's serious loss. Not italicized in casual writing.

distinctions.note: "That's life" is the plain English version; "c'est la vie" sounds lighter and a little more stylish.
Similar acceptance; "it is what it is" can sound more tired or blunt.

examples.everyday: It rained on our picnic, but c'est la vie.
examples.professional: We lost the bid by a few dollars. C'est la vie; on to the next one.
examples.analytical: The narrator's repeated c'est la vie signals resignation rather than real acceptance.

nuance.analogy: Like shrugging your shoulders when the bus pulls away just as you arrive.
nuance.etymology: From French c'est la vie, literally "that is life." It has been common in English since about the early 1900s.
common_mistakes: Spelling it "say la vee" or "c'est la vi."
Saying it in response to someone's tragedy; it can sound uncaring.

senses: The very best people or things of a group; the elite.

etymology: From French crème de la crème, literally "cream of the cream." It came into English in the early 1800s.

conversation.text: These students are the crème de la crème. Only ten percent get in.
Look at us, the crème de la crème of the fantasy league.

core.definition: The very best people or things of a group; the elite.

pronunciation.tip: Say krem duh luh KREM. Both "crème" words rhyme with "them." Do not say "cream."

nuance.connotation: Positive; sometimes used with gentle irony about elitism.
nuance.usage_note: Used for top people or things: "the crème de la crème of Silicon Valley." Often slightly playful. Usually not italicized; the accents are often dropped (creme de la creme). It takes "the": "the crème de la crème of..."
word_family: the cream of the crop (English equivalent)

distinctions.note: Means the same; "cream of the crop" is plain English, "crème de la crème" sounds fancier.
"Elite" is a neutral noun for a top group; "crème de la crème" is more vivid and often affectionate or ironic.

collocations: the crème de la crème of
only the crème de la crème
the crème de la crème of society

examples.everyday: The bakery's croissants are the crème de la crème of the neighborhood.
examples.professional: The conference attracts the crème de la crème of cybersecurity researchers.
examples.analytical: Admissions data show the program draws the crème de la crème of applicants nationwide.

nuance.analogy: Like skimming the top of the milk and then skimming the top of that.
nuance.etymology: From French crème de la crème, literally "cream of the cream." It came into English in the early 1800s.
common_mistakes: Saying "cream de la cream" or spelling it "creme de la cream."
Leaving out "the": say "the crème de la crème."

senses: An unexpected and uncontrollable event, such as a natural disaster or war, that prevents someone from fulfilling a contract and may free them from liability.

etymology: From French force majeure, literally "superior force." It came into English as a legal term in the 1800s.

conversation.text: The hurricane counts as force majeure, so the supplier isn't liable for the delay.
Does our contract have a force majeure clause covering pandemics?

core.definition: An unexpected and uncontrollable event, such as a natural disaster or war, that prevents someone from fulfilling a contract and may free them from liability.

pronunciation.tip: Say fors mah-ZHUR. "Majeure" has the "zh" sound of "measure" and rhymes with "sure" with an r.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical.
nuance.usage_note: Mainly a contract and legal term in American English: "a force majeure clause," "invoke force majeure." It became widely known during the COVID-19 pandemic, when many companies invoked it. Usually not italicized in legal and business writing.

distinctions.note: "Act of God" means a natural disaster beyond human control; "force majeure" is broader and also covers human events like war or strikes.
A breach is a failure to perform without excuse; force majeure is an accepted excuse for not performing.

examples.everyday: The airline called the blizzard force majeure and refused to pay for hotels.
examples.professional: The supplier invoked the force majeure clause after the factory flooded.
examples.analytical: Courts read force majeure clauses narrowly, so events not listed may not qualify.

nuance.analogy: Like a referee stopping a game for lightning: no one is blamed for the interruption.
nuance.etymology: From French force majeure, literally "superior force." It came into English as a legal term in the 1800s.
common_mistakes: Spelling it "force majure" or "force majour."
Assuming any hardship qualifies; usually it must be unforeseeable and named or covered by the contract.

senses: High fashion: expensive, original clothing made by hand and to measure by leading fashion houses; also the houses and designers that make it.

etymology: From French haute couture, literally "high sewing" or "high dressmaking." It came into English in the early 1900s.

conversation.text: That dress is haute couture. It probably cost more than my car.
My Halloween costume is not exactly haute couture.

core.definition: High fashion: expensive, original clothing made by hand and to measure by leading fashion houses; also the houses and designers that make it.

pronunciation.tip: Say oht koo-TOOR. The h is silent: "haute" sounds like "oat."

nuance.connotation: Positive; suggests luxury, artistry, and exclusivity.
nuance.usage_note: Used in fashion writing and in casual talk about luxury: "an haute couture gown," "the haute couture shows in Paris." In France the label is legally protected, but Americans often use it loosely for any high fashion. Not usually italicized. Americans say both "a haute couture" and "an haute couture"; "a haute couture" matches the silent-h pronunciation less well but is common.

distinctions.note: Ready-to-wear (prêt-à-porter) is made in standard sizes; haute couture is made to measure for one client.
"Couture" alone is often used loosely for any designer clothing; "haute couture" is the top, made-to-order level.

examples.everyday: She wore haute couture to the Met Gala.
examples.professional: The brand has stopped producing haute couture and now focuses on ready-to-wear.
examples.analytical: Haute couture accounts for little revenue but shapes the image of luxury fashion houses.

nuance.analogy: Like a hand-built custom car compared with one off the assembly line.
nuance.etymology: From French haute couture, literally "high sewing" or "high dressmaking." It came into English in the early 1900s.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the h ("hot couture"); it is silent: oht.
Spelling it "haut couture" or "haute couteur."

senses: A small decorative object valued for its beauty or craftsmanship, such as a vase, figurine, or ornament.

etymology: From French objet d'art, literally "object of art." It came into English in the mid-1800s.

conversation.text: Her shelves are full of little objets d'art from her travels.
Careful, that coffee mug is basically an objet d'art.

core.definition: A small decorative object valued for its beauty or craftsmanship, such as a vase, figurine, or ornament.

pronunciation.tip: Say awb-zhay DAHR. The t in "objet" and the t in "art" are silent.

nuance.connotation: Positive; suggests taste and refinement, sometimes a little fussy.
nuance.usage_note: Used in antiques, interior design, and auction contexts. Often used in the plural, objets d'art (same pronunciation). Usually not italicized. It refers to small decorative items, not paintings or large sculptures.

distinctions.note: A knickknack is a cheap small ornament; an objet d'art is valued for its artistry.
A work of art can be any size or form; an objet d'art is a small decorative piece.

examples.everyday: The antique shop sells furniture and objets d'art.
examples.professional: The auction includes paintings, jewelry, and objets d'art from the estate.
examples.analytical: Eighteenth-century collectors displayed objets d'art as signs of education and wealth.

nuance.analogy: Like the jewelry of a room: small, but it shows the owner's taste.
nuance.etymology: From French objet d'art, literally "object of art." It came into English in the mid-1800s.
common_mistakes: Writing the plural as "objet d'arts"; it is objets d'art.
Pronouncing it "OB-jet dart."

senses: A small apartment or house kept for occasional use, usually in a city, by someone whose main home is elsewhere.

etymology: From French pied-à-terre, literally "foot on the ground." It came into English in the early 1800s.

conversation.text: They live in Connecticut but keep a pied-à-terre in Manhattan.
Someday I want a little pied-à-terre in Paris.

core.definition: A small apartment or house kept for occasional use, usually in a city, by someone whose main home is elsewhere.

pronunciation.tip: Say pyay duh TAIR. "Pied" is one quick syllable (pyay); some say pee-AY. The d links to "à": duh.

nuance.connotation: Suggests wealth and convenience.
nuance.usage_note: Common in real estate and lifestyle writing, especially about New York, Paris, and London. Some American cities have discussed a "pied-à-terre tax" on such second homes. Written with hyphens; the accent is often dropped (pied-a-terre). Plural: pieds-à-terre.

distinctions.note: A second home can be a vacation house anywhere; a pied-à-terre is usually a small city place for occasional stays.
A vacation home is for leisure; a pied-à-terre is often for work trips or city visits.

examples.everyday: My boss stays in her pied-à-terre downtown during the week.
examples.professional: The listing is marketed as an ideal pied-à-terre for business travelers.
examples.analytical: Housing advocates argue that pied-à-terre purchases reduce the number of homes available to residents.

nuance.analogy: Like a parking spot for your life in the city.
nuance.etymology: From French pied-à-terre, literally "foot on the ground." It came into English in the early 1800s.
common_mistakes: Spelling it without hyphens ("pied a terre") or as "pie de terre."
Using it for a main home; it is a secondary place.

senses: A dance for two people, especially in ballet; also, a close, carefully coordinated interaction between two people or groups.

etymology: From French pas de deux, literally "step of two." It came into English in the 1700s as a ballet term.

conversation.text: The pas de deux in the second act was breathtaking.
The two candidates have been doing a careful pas de deux around the tax issue.

core.definition: A dance for two people, especially in ballet; also, a close, carefully coordinated interaction between two people or groups.

pronunciation.tip: Say pah duh DOO. The s in "pas" and the x in "deux" are silent. A more French ending is closer to "duh" with rounded lips.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; in the figurative sense often suggests delicate maneuvering.
nuance.usage_note: Literally a ballet term; figuratively common in journalism for two parties carefully adjusting to each other, as in negotiations. Usually not italicized. The plural is the same: pas de deux.

distinctions.note: A duet is a musical piece for two; a pas de deux is a dance for two.
"It takes two to tango" stresses shared responsibility; a figurative pas de deux stresses careful coordination.

examples.everyday: Our cats do a funny pas de deux around the food bowl.
examples.professional: Labor and management performed a careful pas de deux before agreeing on a contract.
examples.analytical: Central banks and markets engage in a pas de deux, each reacting to the other's signals.

nuance.analogy: Like two dancers who must know each other's next step before it happens.
nuance.etymology: From French pas de deux, literally "step of two." It came into English in the 1700s as a ballet term.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the s and x ("pass de doox").
Writing the plural as "pas de deuxs."

senses: A style of painting or decoration that makes flat images look so real and three-dimensional that they fool the eye; also, an effect or image made this way.

etymology: From French trompe-l'œil, literally "deceive the eye." It came into English in the late 1800s.

conversation.text: That window on the wall isn't real. It's trompe l'oeil.
The ceiling has a trompe l'oeil sky with clouds and birds.

core.definition: A style of painting or decoration that makes flat images look so real and three-dimensional that they fool the eye; also, an effect or image made this way.

pronunciation.tip: Americans usually say trahmp LOY. Some say tromp LUH-ee, closer to the French.

nuance.connotation: Positive; suggests skill and playful illusion.
nuance.usage_note: Used in art, interior design, and architecture: "a trompe l'oeil mural." It works as a noun and also before a noun as a modifier. American writers most often spell it trompe l'oeil, without a hyphen and with the letters o and e written separately; the French spelling trompe-l'œil, with a hyphen and the joined œ, is also used, especially in art books. Usually not italicized.

distinctions.note: An optical illusion is any trick of perception; trompe l'oeil is an artistic technique for creating one.
Photorealism copies a photo in great detail; trompe l'oeil aims to make you believe the object is really there.

examples.everyday: The bakery painted a trompe l'oeil bookshelf on its back wall.
examples.professional: Our designer suggested a trompe l'oeil arch to make the hallway feel larger.
examples.analytical: Renaissance painters used trompe l'oeil ceilings to make domes appear to open onto the sky.

nuance.analogy: Like a painted door you try to open.
nuance.etymology: From French trompe-l'œil, literally "deceive the eye." It came into English in the late 1800s.
common_mistakes: Spelling it "trompe l'oiel" or "tromp l'oeil"; the French is oeil (eye).
Pronouncing it "tromp lee-OYL."

senses: A sudden, often violent, illegal seizure of government power, usually by a small group such as military officers.

etymology: From French coup d'état, literally "stroke of state." It came into English in the 1600s.

conversation.text: There's been a coup d'état. The army has taken over the capital.
The kids staged a coup d'état and took over the TV remote.

core.definition: A sudden, often violent, illegal seizure of government power, usually by a small group such as military officers.

pronunciation.tip: Say koo day-TAH. The p in "coup" and the final t in "état" are silent.

nuance.connotation: Negative; implies illegitimate force.
nuance.usage_note: Common in news and history. Often shortened to "coup" ("a military coup"). Usually not italicized; the accent is often dropped (coup d'etat). Plural: coups d'état. Figurative and joking uses are common for sudden takeovers in offices or families.

distinctions.note: A revolution is a broad popular uprising that transforms society; a coup d'état is a quick takeover by a small group at the top.
"Coup" can also mean a great success ("a marketing coup"); "coup d'état" always means seizing government.

examples.everyday: My little sister pulled a coup d'état and took the front seat.
examples.professional: The embassy advised citizens to leave after the coup d'état.
examples.analytical: Political scientists find that a coup d'état is more likely after economic shocks.

nuance.analogy: Like a few players grabbing the referee's whistle and declaring themselves in charge of the game.
nuance.etymology: From French coup d'état, literally "stroke of state." It came into English in the 1600s.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the p in "coup" or the t in "état."
Spelling it "coup de tat" or "coup d'etat" without the apostrophe.

senses: In passing; briefly, while talking about something else. In chess, a special capture of a pawn that has just moved two squares.

etymology: From French en passant, literally "in passing." It came into English in the 1600s; the chess sense appeared later.

conversation.text: He mentioned, en passant, that he'd bought a house.
Wait, can you capture en passant here?

core.definition: In passing; briefly, while talking about something else. In chess, a special capture of a pawn that has just moved two squares.

pronunciation.tip: Say ahn pah-SAHN; many Americans pronounce the final t lightly. "En" is a nasal "ahn."

nuance.connotation: Neutral.
nuance.usage_note: Used in writing about a remark made briefly or casually: "mentioned en passant." In chess it is a standard technical term that every player learns. In ordinary American speech, "in passing" is far more common. Usually italicized in general writing, not in chess writing.

distinctions.note: The everyday English equivalent; "en passant" is more literary.
"By the way" introduces a side topic in speech; "en passant" describes a remark made briefly.

examples.everyday: She told me en passant that she's moving to Denver.
examples.professional: The report notes en passant that the budget was overspent.
examples.analytical: The author addresses the economic causes only en passant, focusing instead on politics.

nuance.analogy: Like waving at a friend from a moving car: you acknowledge them without stopping.
nuance.etymology: From French en passant, literally "in passing." It came into English in the 1600s; the chess sense appeared later.
common_mistakes: Spelling it "in passant."
Pronouncing it "en PASS-ant" like English.

senses: A clever, witty remark.

etymology: From French bon mot, literally "good word." It came into English in the 1700s.

conversation.text: She always has a bon mot ready at dinner parties.
His speech was full of bons mots that had everyone laughing.

core.definition: A clever, witty remark.

pronunciation.tip: Say bahn MOH. The t in "mot" is silent. The plural bons mots is said bahn MOHZ.

nuance.connotation: Positive; suggests quick, polished wit.
nuance.usage_note: Used mainly in writing about conversation, speeches, and famous wits: "Oscar Wilde's bons mots." Not very common in casual American speech, where people say "a good line" or "a zinger." Usually not italicized. Plural: bons mots.

distinctions.note: A one-liner is any short joke; a bon mot is a witty, polished remark, often in conversation.
A zinger is a sharp, often cutting joke; a bon mot is witty and elegant, not necessarily cutting.

examples.everyday: Dad ended the toast with a bon mot about marriage and patience.
examples.professional: The CEO's bon mot about "failing fast" ended up on the company's website.
examples.analytical: Biographers often repeat Dorothy Parker's bons mots as evidence of her wit.

nuance.analogy: Like a perfectly timed wink in words.
nuance.etymology: From French bon mot, literally "good word." It came into English in the 1700s.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the t ("bon mott").
Writing the plural as "bon mots"; the standard plural is bons mots.

senses: In cooking, having all ingredients measured, cut, and arranged and all tools ready before you start; more broadly, careful preparation before a task.

etymology: From French mise en place, literally "putting in place." It came into English as a professional kitchen term in the 1900s.

conversation.text: Get your mise en place done before service starts. No chopping during the rush.
I do my mise en place first so I'm not searching for garlic while the oil burns.

core.definition: In cooking, having all ingredients measured, cut, and arranged and all tools ready before you start; more broadly, careful preparation before a task.

pronunciation.tip: Say meez ahn PLAHS. "Mise" sounds like "meez"; "en" is a nasal "ahn."

nuance.connotation: Positive; associated with discipline and organization.
nuance.usage_note: A standard term in professional kitchens, cooking schools, and cooking shows, often shortened to "mise" (meez) by chefs. Home cooks now use it too, and some people use it figuratively for preparing work ("my mise en place for the week"). Usually not italicized in food writing.

distinctions.note: "Prep" is the general word for preparing food; mise en place is the full setup, organized and ready before cooking.
A recipe tells you what to do; mise en place is getting everything ready before you do it.

collocations: set up your mise en place

examples.everyday: I set out my mise en place in little bowls before baking.
examples.professional: New line cooks are judged first on their mise en place.
examples.analytical: Some productivity writers borrow mise en place as a model for preparing a workday.

nuance.analogy: Like laying out all your tools before fixing a bike, so nothing interrupts the job.
nuance.etymology: From French mise en place, literally "putting in place." It came into English as a professional kitchen term in the 1900s.
common_mistakes: Spelling it "mis en place" or "meez en place."
Pronouncing "mise" as "mize."

senses: Used to admit that someone has made a good point against you in an argument; in fencing, used to acknowledge a hit.

etymology: From French touché, literally "touched," called out in fencing to acknowledge a hit. The conversational use spread in English in the early 1900s.

conversation.text: "You say I'm messy, but your car is worse." "Touché."
Okay, touché. I did forget your birthday too.

core.definition: Used to admit that someone has made a good point against you in an argument; in fencing, used to acknowledge a hit.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable: too-SHAY. The "ch" is "sh."

nuance.connotation: Good-humored; a gracious or playful admission of a fair point.
nuance.usage_note: Very common in casual American conversation and texting as a one-word reply to a clever comeback. It is good-natured and admits the point without full surrender. In fencing it is a technical term for a hit. Often written without the accent (touche), but then it can be confused with the English word "touch"; keep the accent when you can.

distinctions.note: "Fair point" is plain and sincere; "touché" is playful and admits you were caught out by a clever reply.
"Touchy" means easily offended; "touché" admits a point. They are unrelated in meaning.

examples.everyday: "You never cook." "You never clean." "Touché."
examples.professional: When the client pointed out our own report contradicted us, all I could say was "touché."
examples.analytical: The debater's quick touché disarmed her opponent and drew applause.

nuance.analogy: Like a fencer's opponent saluting after a clean hit.
nuance.etymology: From French touché, literally "touched," called out in fencing to acknowledge a hit. The conversational use spread in English in the early 1900s.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it "TOOSH" or "TOO-shee."
Using it to make your own point; you say it when the other person has scored.
